user.t:
Council position (read-only, concise) on: take all 11 pre-product B2B SaaS marketing sites LIVE via GitHub Pages? Facts: 11 PRIVATE repos; private-repo Pages needs a PAID plan; free Pages only serves PUBLIC repos. Each repo has a static site under marketing/site/ (zero-dependency Node build -> static HTML) with placeholder SITE_URL/CONTACT_EMAIL. Alternative: a separate PUBLIC "<name>-site" repo per business with only the built static site + a Pages deploy workflow (actions/deploy-pages), keeping business code private.
From the devops/deployment lens: the concrete mechanics — how to deploy each static site to Pages, the build/deploy workflow, enabling Pages (settings/API), custom domain vs <user>.github.io/<repo>, the private-repo-paid constraint, and exactly what needs to change (SITE_URL = the real Pages URL, CONTACT_EMAIL). Which approach is operationally cleanest and lowest-risk? Concise, honest. Return a short position + recommended mechanism + preconditions.

handback.t:
## Operator Position: Pages for 11 pre-product marketing sites

**Core recommendation:** Use the separate PUBLIC "<name>-site" repo per business, with only built static output plus a Pages deploy workflow. It is the only zero-cost path that keeps business code private. Do NOT make the 11 main repos public. Upgrading to a paid plan only to host pre-product placeholder sites is poor value unless you already pay for it. (From general GitHub knowledge, not verified live here: Pages on private repos needs Pro/Team/Enterprise, and free Pages serves public repos only. Please confirm current plan terms.)

**Caveat on what "private" means:** Pages sites are always publicly reachable, even when built from a private repo. So the site content is public either way. Only the source stays private. That means no secrets, no internal pricing, no roadmap in marketing/site/.

**Recommended mechanism (per business, identical, scriptable)**
1. Create the public repo `<user>/<name>-site` (gh repo create --public).
2. In the private repo, run the zero-dependency Node build with SITE_URL and CONTACT_EMAIL set. This produces static HTML.
3. Publish the output into the public repo. Two options:
   - Simplest and lowest-risk: a one-time or on-demand script (`build -> copy dist/ to public repo -> git push`). The public repo holds only built HTML, and the workflow just uploads it. This keeps zero secrets and zero cross-repo credentials. Good for pre-product sites that change rarely.
   - Automated: a workflow in the private repo that builds and pushes to the public repo. This needs a fine-grained PAT or deploy key stored as a secret in the private repo. Defer this until the third manual update ("automate the third time").
4. Public repo workflow `.github/workflows/pages.yml`: trigger on push to main plus workflow_dispatch, with permissions `contents: read, pages: write, id-token: write`, and a concurrency group. Steps: actions/checkout, actions/configure-pages, actions/upload-pages-artifact (path `.`, or the dist dir), then a deploy job using actions/deploy-pages with environment `github-pages`.
5. Enable Pages with source = GitHub Actions. Via API: `gh api -X POST repos/<user>/<name>-site/pages -f build_type=workflow`. If it already exists, use PUT. The UI path is Settings > Pages > Source: GitHub Actions. The first deploy fails if Pages is not enabled, so this must come before the first push or a re-run.
6. Verify: curl -I the URL, check the Actions run, and confirm that deploy-pages reports the page_url.

**URL and the SITE_URL change (the main gotcha)**
- Without a custom domain, a project site lives at `https://<user>.github.io/<name>-site/`. This is a subpath. Any root-absolute links (`/style.css`, `/about`) will break. The build must either use relative links or honor a base path. Check the build for hardcoded absolute paths before going live.
- Set SITE_URL to exactly `https://<user>.github.io/<name>-site` (decide on trailing-slash handling, and keep it consistent). This feeds canonical tags, og:url, sitemap.xml and robots.txt. Rebuild after setting it, since a wrong value ships bad canonicals and an index-pointing sitemap.
- Custom domain is cleaner (root path, so SITE_URL = `https://www.<domain>`, no base-path trouble). Mechanics: add a CNAME file in the output, or set the domain via the API or UI; use a CNAME DNS record to `<user>.github.io` for subdomains or A/AAAA records to GitHub's IPs for apex, then enable Enforce HTTPS after the cert is issued. Verifying the domain at the account level prevents takeover. Domains cost money and 11 of them multiplies the DNS toil, so for pre-product validation `github.io` subpaths are acceptable. Move to custom domains per business only as it gets traction.
- Alternative without subpath pain: name the repo `<user>.github.io`. Only one such repo exists per account, so it is not usable for 11 sites. Under an org per business it is possible, but that is extra overhead.

**CONTACT_EMAIL**
- Needs a real, monitored address per business before launch. A mailto on a public page will be scraped, so use a dedicated alias or forwarding address rather than a personal inbox. Check that every site renders it (footer, contact page, any mailto or form action). Pre-product sites should state honestly that the product is not yet available (waitlist or early access), not imply live service.

**Why this beats the alternatives**
- Paid private-repo Pages: recurring cost, no extra isolation, since the output is public anyway.
- Making main repos public: leaks business code, which is the exact thing to avoid.
- Separate public site repo: free, small blast radius (the repo contains only already-public content), easy rollback via `git revert` and redeploy. Cost is 11 extra repos to maintain. This is minor for a scripted setup.
- Other hosts (Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel) can deploy from private repos for free and would avoid the extra repos. Mentioned as an option only because you asked about GitHub Pages. They also have clean preview deploys.

**Preconditions (checklist before any go-live)**
- [ ] Decide the plan: free + public site repos (recommended) vs. a paid plan.
- [ ] Audit marketing/site/ and the built output for secrets, internal names, emails, or anything not meant to be public. Run secret scanning on each public repo.
- [ ] Confirm the build emits relative or base-path-aware links, and test under a subpath locally (`npx serve` with a prefix, or open the built files).
- [ ] Set real SITE_URL (the exact Pages URL, or custom domain) and CONTACT_EMAIL, then rebuild. Verify canonical, og:url, sitemap.xml and robots.txt all point to the real URL.
- [ ] Create the public repos, enable Pages with build_type=workflow, push, and confirm the first deploy is green.
- [ ] Check the placeholder content is honest (pre-product, no fake customers, testimonials, logos or metrics). Check legal minimums for B2B: privacy notice if any form or analytics is used.
- [ ] Optional monitoring: a free uptime check (UptimeRobot or a scheduled workflow curl) and Search Console. Do not over-instrument 11 pre-product pages.
- [ ] Script it once (gh repo create, Pages API, copy, push) and loop over the 11 repos. Do a pilot on 1 site first, then roll out to the other 10.

**Risks if ignored**
- Subpath breakage: root-absolute links render unstyled or 404 on github.io/<repo>/.
- Wrong SITE_URL: canonicals and sitemap point at placeholders, which hurts indexing.
- Accidentally publishing private material when copying into the public repo.

**Dependencies on other domains:** Craftsman or build owner for base-path-safe links; Guardian/legal for public-content and privacy review; whoever owns email for the CONTACT_EMAIL aliases.

I did not inspect the actual repos or the build script here. Statements about plan limits and API calls come from general knowledge and should be spot-checked before the rollout.
